Through long-term and repeated practice, it becomes stable in the eternal.
Afterwards, there is no pain in the body, nor is old age ever seen; perfected and endowed with all virtues, he remains amidst various afflictions;
always maintaining his secret signs, he dwells in the midst of the forest.
The subtle body (sūkṣmaśarīra) of living beings appears in various ways;
since its majesty is inconceivable, one should not despise it.
The one lacking faith, the evil-minded, the nihilist, the one whose doubts are unsettled,
the rationalist, and the hypocrite— Yoga is not within their reach.
Those base individuals who do not know his divine play and instead utter insults against this Lord of Yogis— those most sinful ones will certainly fall into hell.
People should not even entertain doubt regarding the bodies of yogis;
for they sport in the midst of the world just like an ordinary man.
O Pārvatī, those who utter insults against the Lord of Yogins, against Yoga, or against the Yoga-śāstra, are Rākṣasas because of that; they are indeed demons.
Those who are heretics, devoted to sin, and averse to their own duty—
they by whom the yogi has been insulted— for them there shall be no protector on this earth.
O lady of virtuous vows, the life-span, luster, fame, and merit of that person perish,
whose mind, even when engaged in yoga, becomes fixed upon the form of liberation.
Yoga that is contrary to one's own dharma does not please him;
he too becomes an embryo and experiences suffering incessantly.
In the conditioned.
(3) Listen now to the eighty-four thousand supreme postures; among them,
that which was proclaimed by the Primordial Lord is here called the lotus posture (padmāsana).
Having carefully placed the feet flat and the thighs together,
and likewise having placed the hands flat upon the middle of the thighs, one should then fix the gaze.
The wise man should place [the tongue] at the tip of the nose and against the roots of the teeth;
having pressed the chin against the chest, he should slowly settle the breath.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which destroys all diseases;
it is difficult for anyone to attain, yet it is found on earth by the wise.
O Sāṃkṛti, knower of reality, listen attentively as I describe to you the sequence for the practice of yoga,
together with the defining characteristics of the various yogas.
Whether young or very old, or even afflicted by disease,
one who is untiring attains perfection through gradual practice in all yogas.
Whether he be a Brahmin, a Śramaṇa, or even a Buddhist, whether he has fallen from his status,
or be a Kāpālika or a Cārvāka— provided he is wise and endowed with faith.
One who constantly delights in the practice of yoga shall attain all perfections;
for one who is engaged in action, success will come to pass, but how could it be for one who is inactive?
The perfection of yoga is not produced by the mere recitation of treatises.
Whether one is shaven-headed or wears a turban, whether clad in saffron robes or even matted-haired with ashes smeared upon him, he is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Whether he is one who recites the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya," or one who performs external worship,
adorned with the twelve places, the rosary, and many ornaments;
How can one who is devoid of ritual action, or one who is cruel, attain perfection? Wearing the [divine] form is the cause of perfection; how is that so?
O Sāṅkṛti, it is true that ritual action alone is the cause of perfection.
Those who practice yoga for the sake of the genitals and the belly, while claiming to possess the mastery of yoga,
indeed deceive people by being devoid of actual spiritual practice.
p.
4) Having gradually recognized those who are high and low, deluded by deception, devoted to yoga, yet devoid of the practice of yoga— knowing them to be of such a kind— [one should avoid them].
One should never deceive those who assume disguises for the sake of their own interests;
for such beings are always obstacles to the practice of yoga.
One should especially avoid such actions that arise from [the pursuit of] supernatural powers;
for at the time of initial practice, O Sage, various forms of negligence occur. (16)
Laziness is the first obstacle; the second is proclaimed to be the company of the aforementioned rogues; and the third is the practice of mantra.
The fourth is the doctrine of the elements (dhātuvāda), and the fifth is the doctrine of the stages (kakṣyāvāda);
thus, O Sage, there are many such obstacles, equal to a mirage.
When these arise for one who has mastered the steady posture, the wise man should recognize them and abandon them;
thereafter, he himself should perform *prāṇāyāma* while seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).
He should construct a very beautiful hut with a narrow door and free from cracks.
It should be carefully smeared daily with cow dung or whitewash, and kept free from bedbugs, mosquitoes, and spiders.
It was thoroughly swept with a broom, untiringly;
it was perfumed with fragrant scents and incensed with guggulu and other resins.
It was [cleansed] of the eighteen impurities, including the urges of feces, urine, and so forth.
It should be free from food that is spoiled or mixed with mouthfuls of other things;
it should not be too high nor too low, and it must be kept away from contact with others.
Having spread out a waveless seat in that monastery,
the wise man, seated there in the lotus posture (padmāsana),
with his body straight and palms joined in reverence, should bow to his chosen deities.
Then, having restrained Piṅgalā with the thumb of the right hand,
one should slowly fill the wind through the iḍā.
Then, one should perform the *kumbhaka* (retention) by means of suppression according to one's capacity.
5) Again, one should exhale through the Piṅgalā very slowly and not with force;
then, having filled [the breath] through the Piṅgalā, one should fill the abdomen slowly.
Having retained [the breath] according to one's capacity, one should exhale it slowly through the iḍā;
one should retain it without obstruction, both while exhaling and while filling.
In this manner, one should perform it in the morning twenty times according to one's capacity;
this is known as the *sahita* breath-retention (*kumbhaka*), which is free from all planetary afflictions.
In this very manner, at midnight as well, one should again perform twenty kumbhakas,
together with rechaka and pūraka, every day.
Therefore, the Sahita Kumbhaka consists of [the breath] together with Rechaka and Pūraka;
one should practice this for three months, after which the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śuddhi) occurs.
But when the purification of the channels has occurred, then signs arise externally upon the body of the yogin; those I shall describe in their entirety.
Lightness of the body, a glow from the fire residing in the stomach, and emaciation of the body will certainly arise at that time. (17)
Likewise, I shall describe the foods that quickly lead to success in yoga:
milk, ghee, sweet food, and a moderate diet are recommended.
At the time previously mentioned, one should perform the practice of breath control (pavana-abhyāsa);
thereafter, one will possess the power to retain the breath for as long as desired.
Through the mastery of breath-retention (dhāraṇā) according to one's will, the pure kumbhaka is accomplished; when the pure kumbhaka, devoid of exhalation and inhalation, is mastered.
Nothing whatsoever in the three worlds is difficult to obtain there;
first perspiration arises, and therefore one should cause it to be massaged.
Furthermore, from that very practice of breath-retention (dhāraṇā), performed gradually and ever more slowly,
the body of that yogi becomes light while seated.
From practice even more intense than that, one certainly becomes difficult to overcome;
just as the *dadhadru* leaps up again and again while making a loud noise upon the ground.
The yogi established in the lotus posture likewise moves upon the ground;
through even more intense practice, the abandonment of the ground occurs.
Remaining in the lotus posture (padmāsana), he exists without touching the ground;
indeed, being without support, he attains such a wonderful power.
Whether he has not eaten or has already eaten, the yogi is not distressed;
his urine and feces become scant, his sleep becomes minimal,
and the saliva, sweat, and breath of his mouth become free from foul odors.
From that point onward, these [faults] never arise in him again;
through even more intense practice, a great power is produced.
By means of which one may attain the siddhi of moving upon the earth, becoming capable of conquering those who roam the earth—
whether it be a tiger, a buffalo, a wild beast, a gayal, or even an elephant.
Or that yogi dies like a lion; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, due to negligence, a great obstacle may arise for the yogi. O Noble One, those who are under the sway of that form desire his company.
If he indeed forms an attachment, his drop perishes.
The exhaustion of life-span, the loss of seminal drops, and the incapacity of the vital fluids arise [from this];
therefore, one should diligently practice the avoidance of association with women.
A fragrant scent shall constantly arise from the limbs of the yogin due to the retention of the *bindu*.
Therefore, with every effort, the protection of the *bindu* is indeed the duty of the yogin. Then, seated in a secluded place, he should recite the *praṇava* with a protracted (*pluta*) measure.
One should recite it for the destruction of previously accumulated sins;
this Praṇava is the remover of all obstacles and the destroyer of all defects.
Thus, through the yoga of practice, perfection arises from the initial undertaking;
thereafter, the state of the "jar" (ghaṭāvasthā) occurs constantly from the practice of breath control (pavana).
Since the prāṇa, apāna, mind, and vital air of both the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) have attained unity through mutual purification within the "pot" (ghaṭa),
therefore the state known as the "pot" is traditionally remembered by yogins as well-established.
I shall describe in their entirety those signs that may appear therein;
one should completely abandon the previously mentioned practice after the fourth [stage].
Whether by day or by night, one should practice for at least one watch (yāma);
one may perform the *kevala-kumbhaka* alone once.
Indeed, O Lord, the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) is possible for the yogi through this *yama*.
When a yogi, having resorted to breath-retention (kumbhaka), personally withdraws the senses from the objects of the senses, that is called withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Whatever one sees with the two eyes, one should contemplate that as the Self;
whatever one hears with the two ears, one should contemplate that as the Self.
Whatever one smells with the nose, one should contemplate that as the Self;
whatever one tastes with the tongue, one should contemplate that as the Self.
Whatever is touched by the skin, the yogi should contemplate that very thing as the Self.
In this manner, the yogi, free from sloth, should diligently practice every day for the duration of one watch (yāma) to contemplate the respective number of each of the organs of perception.
Then, manifold powers arise intensely for the yogin:
far-sight, far-hearing, and likewise the ability to travel to distant places in an instant;
indeed, the state of moving through the sky arises from the yoga of constant practice.
In this way, the wise among yogins should conduct themselves for the sake of attaining yoga-perfection;
these are the obstacles to great accomplishment, and the wise man should remain alert toward them.
One should never display one's own power to the world;
however, one may occasionally show it out of affection to one who is endowed with devotion.
Just as one who is free, just as one who is deluded, or just as one who is deaf,
so should one conduct oneself in the worlds for the sake of protecting one's own power.
p.
8) Indeed, many disciples who act for their own benefit will undoubtedly request the Lord of Yogins for their respective purposes.
Due to that extremely fierce causal karma, one's own habitual practice may be forgotten;
deprived of such practice, one consequently falls into the state of worldly existence.
Without forgetting the words of the guru, one should practice day and night;
through the yoga of constant practice, the state of the jar (ghaṭāvasthā) will thus come to be.
Through lack of practice, that very [state] becomes futile, and the assemblies do not succeed;
therefore, one should practice yoga itself with every effort.
From that, through the yoga of practice, the stage of proficiency arises.
Since the wind is well-acquainted with the kuṇḍalinī, it awakens her together with the fire and enters the suṣumnā without opposition.
Together with the vital wind, the mind should enter the Great Path;
for the Great Path, the cremation ground, and the Suṣumnā are indeed one and the same.
There is only a difference in name according to other traditions, and a difference in result that exists [therein].
The present and the future are indeed enveloped by that which is near to the past;
whose manifold manifestation, being well-favored, enters here.
One should diligently understand the objects to be meditated upon;
through yoga, one should perform the five-fold concentration which removes the fear of each respective element.
One should perform the *ghuṭikā* concentration fivefold, from below the navel to above the anus;
through this concentration on the earth element, one attains mastery over the winds and is freed from fear of them.
"Death shall not arise from the earth for this yogi"—
this is the earth-dhāraṇā.
Then one should hold the breath at the location of the navel for five nāḍikās.
Just as fire does not burn the body of one who possesses the fire-mantra, so too death does not consume him;
his body remains established within the circle of fire—this is the concentration on fire (agnidhāraṇā).
O Vāyu, by holding the breath for five ghaṭikās in the space measured between the navel, the eyebrows, and the nose— these three points— the remnants of the vital air are indeed purified.
(9) "By means of the retention [of breath], let there be no fear for the yogin from the two winds. Thus ends the retention of the winds.
The yogi should hold the breath with effort for five *nāḍikās* above the center of the eyebrows;
this is the space-concentration (*ākāśa-dhāraṇā*). Performing the concentration on space, one conquers death in a marvelous way;
remaining wherever one may be, one enjoys ultimate happiness. Thus are the five kinds of elemental concentrations.

For one who practices *bhūtadhāraṇā* (the retention of the elements), even until the dissolution of Brahmā, death does not exist for him. Then, having restrained the vital air (*vāyu*), one should practice meditation (*dhyāna*) for exactly sixty *ghaṭikās*, focusing on the deity of the syllable *A* who bestows desired boons. This meditation with attributes (*saguṇa-dhyāna*) bestows qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest.

Having meditated upon the attributeless as being like space, one enters the path of liberation. One should practice this meditation on the attributeless and then cultivate *samādhi*; within twelve days alone, one may attain *samādhi*. By restraining the vital breath (*vāyu*), the wise man becomes firmly liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). *Samādhi* is the state of equanimity; [it pertains to] the individual self (*jīvātman*).
Of the two supreme selves.
If one desires to cast off one's own body, one should depart by oneself;
having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma, they merge into the Supreme Brahman.
If one were not willing to relinquish one's own dear body,
one might wander through all the worlds, endowed with the primary qualities beginning with liberality.
Sometimes, by his own will, he may become a body even in heaven;
or, by his own will, through a mere glance, he may become a man or a woman.
By his own will, he may become a lion, a tiger, or an elephant, or he may go among living beings as he desires;
indeed, whatever the Yogin wishes for, that very thing he assumes, just like Maheśvara.
This path of the monkey has been described to you according to the eightfold Yoga practiced by the refined.
Then, O King, yoga will certainly arise without any interval;
success does not come through mere consciousness alone, but is born from practice alone.
Having attained the state of Rājayoga, which brings all sentient beings under one's influence, one may do everything or do nothing at all, according to one's specific inclination.
But when the activity of the yogins is perfected through the royal yoga (rājayoga),
then the state perfected therein is the Unmanifested (unmanī), whose nature is bliss.
The perfected yogis shall bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon him;
O Brahmin, having reflected upon everything thus calculated, one should practice yoga.
Having attained all perfections through the grace of our Dattātreya,
whoever recites this daily in this manner and tells it to the virtuous,
for them yoga will surely be accomplished through the very sequence of practice; of this there is no doubt.
Yogins who are intensely devoted to practice, whether in forests or in houses,
truly find delight for a long time, being devoid of the company of worldly crowds.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice yoga together with its constituent limbs.
The practice of yoga bears fruit in this very life, while other actions are fruitless.
By the power of Mahāmāyā, may there be the bliss of consciousness for all;
since every effort is dependent upon Her, one should therefore worship Her alone.
Thus ends the *Dattātreyabodha*.
Hari Oṃ.
May there be auspiciousness.
